```{r library}
library(terroir)
```

## Why

A grower or agronomist assembling covariates for a trial site asks a plain
question: for one exact paddock, can I pull daily temperature and rainfall,
a vegetation index, and district farm economics from several public
archives, through one interface, and get back a tidy table that carries its
own source, licence and retrieval time, without leaking the paddock's exact
coordinates and without a live network connection standing between me and
reproducing the analysis next season? This vignette answers with terroir's
own shipped fixtures, offline throughout, and closes on what happens when a
source cannot answer at all.

## What

`terroir` pulls climate, weather, vegetation-index, soil, elevation and
agricultural-economics data for a single geographic point from many free
sources, behind one uniform request-and-response contract. It is the
data-collector member of the ORCHESTRA: a producer that feeds covariates and
forcings to downstream modelling. Every source is an optional adapter, so
terroir installs and works with none of the source packages present.

`geo_point_request()` builds a request: a point, an optional date range, the
variables wanted, and the id of one registered source. `list_sources()`
lists every registered adapter, and `register_source()` adds one, enforcing
the data-collector role's free-only rule -- an adapter that does not reach a
free source is refused at registration time, not discovered later as a
billing surprise. `collect_point()` dispatches one request to its adapter
and returns a verified `geo_point_series`, or a structured refusal when the
source is unknown, its package is missing, the point falls outside the
source's declared coverage, or a returned value fails a plausibility check.
`collect_points()` runs a whole batch of requests at once and keeps every
refusal as an accounted row rather than dropping it from the stack.
`is_refusal()` and `is_replayed()` tell the two special outcomes apart from
an ordinary series; `verify_geo_series()` and `geo_point_schema()` are the
contract itself, exported so a downstream package can check or type against
them directly rather than reaching into terroir's internals.

## Do

### The registered sources

```{r sources}
src <- list_sources()
nrow(src)
```

```{r sources-kable, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  src[, .(id, package, free)],
  caption = "Every source adapter terroir currently registers."
)
```

Every adapter is free -- the data-collector role forbids a paid source,
enforced by `register_source()` itself rather than merely documented.

### Registering a new source

The toy adapter below returns a constant value for illustration; a real
adapter would call an upstream package instead, the way the built-in
sources do.

```{r register-toy}
toy_adapter <- function(request, retrieved_at) {
  dt <- data.table::data.table(
    date = request$start, variable = "toy_index", value = 1
  )
  new_geo_point_series(
    dt, lon = request$lon, lat = request$lat, source = "toy_local",
    source_version = "1.0", license = "CC0", retrieved_at = retrieved_at,
    call = "toy_adapter()"
  )
}
register_source(
  "toy_local", toy_adapter, package = "base", free = TRUE,
  description = "Illustrative in-memory adapter used only in this vignette"
)
"toy_local" %in% list_sources()$id
```

The free-only rule is enforced, not merely stated: registering the same
adapter under `free = FALSE` is refused outright, and the refusal names the
rule it enforces.

```{r register-paid}
free_only_refusal <- tryCatch(
  register_source("toy_paid", toy_adapter, package = "base", free = FALSE),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
cat(free_only_refusal)
```

### A request

```{r request}
req <- geo_point_request(
  lon = 138.6, lat = -34.92,       # Adelaide
  start = "2020-01-01", end = "2020-01-31",
  variables = c("T2M", "PRECTOTCORR"),
  source = "nasapower"
)
req
```

### Collecting (live)

`collect_point()` performs the download. It is not run here (this vignette
builds offline), but the call is simply:

```{r live-not-run, eval = FALSE}
series <- collect_point(req)
series                 # a geo_point_series: tidy data.table + provenance
attr(series, "provenance")
```

### Offline replay (zero network)

`terroir` ships a small set of recorded fixtures, one per CORE source.
Passing `offline = TRUE` answers a request from the matching fixture with no
network egress at all -- useful for a reproducible pipeline, for a
continuous-integration run, and (with coarsening, below) for a sovereign
coordinate that must never reach an upstream service. A replayed series
carries `replayed = TRUE` in its provenance and keeps the recording's
`retrieved_at`, so a consumer can always tell a cached series from a live
one.

```{r offline-collect}
offline_req <- geo_point_request(
  lon = 138.6, lat = -34.92,
  start = "2020-01-01", end = "2020-01-10",
  variables = c("T2M", "PRECTOTCORR"),
  source = "nasapower"
)
series <- collect_point(offline_req, offline = TRUE)
is_replayed(series)
attr(series, "provenance")$retrieved_at   # the fixture's stamp, not now
head(series, 3)
```

Offline mode needs none of the source packages installed: it reads `.rds`
fixtures and never touches an adapter. When no recorded fixture answers a
request, offline mode returns a structured refusal rather than silently
falling back to the network -- the zero-egress guarantee is absolute. A
caller can point terroir at their own directory of recorded fixtures with
`options(terroir.fixture_dir = "/path/to/fixtures")`, or switch the whole
session offline with `options(terroir.offline = TRUE)`.

### A figure: what the replayed series looked like

A `geo_point_series` is long (one row per date x variable), so plotting it
as small multiples -- one panel per variable, sharing the date axis -- is
the natural way to look at what a collector call actually returned.

```{r fig-offline-series, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), echo = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.cap = "Adelaide, 1-10 January 2020, replayed from the shipped NASA POWER fixture: daily mean air temperature at 2 m and daily total precipitation. No network call was made to produce this figure."}
panel_lab <- c(
  T2M = "air temperature at 2 m (degC)",
  PRECTOTCORR = "total precipitation (mm)"
)
plot_dt <- data.table::copy(series)
plot_dt[, panel := panel_lab[variable]]
ggplot2::ggplot(
  plot_dt, ggplot2::aes(x = date, y = value, colour = variable)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1L, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "date", y = "daily value") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

```{r fig-offline-series-skip, echo = FALSE, eval = !requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), results = "asis"}
cat("ggplot2 is not installed; the replayed-series figure is skipped.\n")
```

### Sovereign coordinates (coarsening)

A grower's exact paddock GPS is sensitive. When a point is flagged
`sovereign = TRUE`, `terroir` coarsens the coordinate to roughly a
one-kilometre cell before any upstream call, so the exact location never
leaves the host. Both the raw-requested and the coarsened-sent coordinate
are recorded in provenance -- the host keeps the full record, the upstream
service sees only the coarsened point.

```{r sovereign}
sovereign_req <- geo_point_request(
  lon = 138.63124, lat = -34.92871,   # an exact paddock GPS
  start = "2020-01-01", end = "2020-01-31",
  source = "nasapower",
  sovereign = TRUE                    # coarsening on by default
)
sovereign_req       # prints both the raw and the coarsened (sent) point
```

Coarsening is also available for a non-sovereign point via the `coarsen`
argument: a single number rounds to that many degrees of precision (for
example `coarsen = 0.01` for a roughly 1 km cell), and
`coarsen = list(grid = 0.25)` snaps each coordinate to the nearest
quarter-degree grid node. The returned series' provenance gains
`sovereign`, `coarsen_policy`, and the raw-vs-sent coordinates; the fixed
ten-column series schema is unchanged, so a consumer reading those columns
is unaffected.

### The response contract

```{r schema}
geo_point_schema()
```

Every series carries these ten columns plus a mandatory provenance
attribute (source, version, retrieval time, licence, the exact upstream
call); `verify_geo_series()` checks both and fails loudly if either is
missing, so a malformed series never flows downstream silently.

```{r verify}
verify_geo_series(series)
```

The `unit` column is part of the contract but is not yet populated by every
adapter: `nasapower` and `abares` emit `NA_character_` there, and so does
`nert` for actual evapotranspiration, whose unit is ambiguous upstream. The
vegetation-index sources set `"index"`, and `silo`, `worldclim`, `elevation`,
`soilgrids`, `chirps` and the other `nert` products set a physical unit.
`verify_geo_series()` does not yet warn on an all-`NA` `unit` column.

### Graceful refusal

If a source's package is not installed, or its free key is unset, a caller
gets a first-class refusal rather than an error.

```{r refusal}
refused <- suppressWarnings(
  collect_point(geo_point_request(0, 0, source = "not_a_source"))
)
is_refusal(refused)
refused
```

### Batch collection

`collect_points()` runs several requests at once and stacks the outcomes
into one table, tagged with a `request_index` and a `status` column. A
refusal contributes exactly one accounted row rather than disappearing from
the stack, so a multi-site collection with a dead source still reports
every request it was given.

```{r batch}
batch_reqs <- list(
  geo_point_request(
    138.6, -34.92, "2020-01-01", "2020-01-10",
    variables = c("T2M", "PRECTOTCORR"), source = "nasapower"
  ),
  geo_point_request(140.7, -35.30, source = "abares"),
  geo_point_request(0, 0, source = "not_a_source")
)
batch_out <- collect_points(batch_reqs, offline = TRUE)
batch_summary <- batch_out[, .(
  source = source[1L], status = status[1L], n_rows = .N,
  reason = reason[1L]
), by = request_index]
```

```{r batch-kable, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  batch_summary,
  caption = paste0(
    "One row per request in a three-request batch (n = ", nrow(batch_out),
    " stacked rows in total)."
  )
)
```

### Sources at a glance

```{r sources-table, echo = FALSE}
sources_table <- data.table::data.table(
  id = c("nasapower", "silo", "abares", "modis", "stac", "nert", "ocular",
         "isric", "worldclim", "elevation", "soilgrids", "chirps"),
  upstream = c(
    "nasapower", "weatherOz", "read.abares", "MODISTools", "rsi",
    "nert (AAGI-AUS)", "ocular (AAGI-AUS)", "apsimx", "geodata", "geodata",
    "geodata", "chirps"
  ),
  domain = c(
    "global climate + solar (no key)",
    "SILO 5 km grid, Australia (free email key)",
    "Australian gridded farm economics",
    "MODIS NDVI/EVI",
    "Sentinel-2 NDVI via Planetary Computer",
    paste0(
      "TERN soil, soil-moisture, AET, canopy height, phenology ",
      "(Australia; free key)"
    ),
    paste0(
      "Sentinel-2 / Landsat spectral-index series over a 500 m window ",
      "(Planetary Computer; cloud-masked, no key)"
    ),
    "SoilGrids soil profile by depth layer (global, no key)",
    "WorldClim 2.1 bioclimatic variables bio_1 to bio_19 (global, no key)",
    "SRTM 90 m elevation and slope (non-commercial licence, no key)",
    "SoilGrids 2.0 means at 0-60 cm in four depths (CC BY 4.0, no key)",
    "CHIRPS 2.0 daily rainfall, 50 S to 50 N (public domain, no key)"
  )
)
knitr::kable(
  sources_table,
  caption = "The registered sources and what each covers."
)
```

The `ocular` source takes its index name from `variables[1]` (default
`"NDVI"`) and its sensor from `variables[2]` (`"auto"`, `"sentinel-2"`,
`"landsat-8"` or `"landsat-5"`; `"auto"` by default). Pixel cloud masking is
on and cannot be switched off: a date whose window is entirely cloud is
dropped from the series rather than returned as a spurious near-zero index.

`worldclim`, `elevation`, `soilgrids` and `chirps` answer many requests in
one upstream call when `collect_points()` is given a batch, so a set of
sites costs one raster read rather than one per site. `worldclim` and
`elevation` carry non-commercial licences that appear in each series'
provenance. GSODR is enrolled in the ORCHESTRA and lands as an adapter in a
future release.

## Read

```{r read-prep, echo = FALSE}
temp_dt <- series[series$variable == "T2M", ]
precip_dt <- series[series$variable == "PRECTOTCORR", ]
temp_min <- min(temp_dt$value)
temp_max <- max(temp_dt$value)
precip_wet <- precip_dt[precip_dt$value > 0, ]
```

`r nrow(src)` sources are currently registered, all free by construction:
the free-only rule tested above refuses a paid adapter with an explicit
error rather than letting one slip into the registry silently.

Air temperature at Adelaide across the replayed ten days ranges from
`r sprintf("%.2f", temp_min)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", temp_max)` degC -- a
day-to-day swing typical of Adelaide midsummer once a front moves through --
while precipitation is essentially dry:
`r nrow(precip_wet)` of the ten days record a trace
(`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", precip_wet$value), collapse = " and ")` mm), and
the rest are zero. A collector that returned a flat temperature line or a
wet run of days here would be the signal to distrust the fixture before
trusting anything built on top of it.

Coarsening moves the sovereign point from its exact
(`r sovereign_req$lon_raw`, `r sovereign_req$lat_raw`) to the sent
(`r sovereign_req$lon`, `r sovereign_req$lat`) under the
`r sovereign_req$coarsen_policy` policy -- roughly a one-kilometre cell at
this latitude -- so only the coarsened point, never the exact paddock GPS,
reaches the upstream service.

The three-request batch stacks `r nrow(batch_out)` rows: the two answerable
requests (`nasapower`, `abares`) each contribute one row per collected
value, and the one unregistered source contributes exactly one refused row
rather than being dropped, carrying its own reason in the `reason` column
rather than a bare `NA`.

## Limits

The five CORE-source fixtures shipped with this vignette (`nasapower`,
`silo`, `modis`, `abares`, `stac`) were recorded once, on 2 June 2026: they
answer exactly the point, date range and variables recorded in the fixture
manifest, and read nothing live, so the temperature and precipitation
figures above describe that one recorded January rather than current
conditions. `nert` and `ocular` ship no offline fixture in this package, so
neither their live retrieval nor `ocular`'s cloud masking is exercised
here; `NEWS.md` documents both in full. `silo`, `abares` and `nert` refuse a
point outside Australia's bounding box, and `ocular` refuses outside its
UTM-defined latitude band, because its window is built in UTM and is
undefined further poleward -- neither restriction is exercised in this
vignette, whose one worked point sits well inside every source's coverage.
Coordinate coarsening rounds to a fixed number of decimal degrees or snaps
to a grid; it is not a true geodesic buffer, so the ground distance a
coarsened point actually moves varies with latitude rather than being a
constant one kilometre everywhere. Several of the external facts this
package asserts remain unverified against their own authority -- among them
the SILO variable codes, the ABARES layer-name dictionary and the
Sentinel-2 band mapping -- and `terroir_external_facts()` and
`terroir_fact_status()` enumerate exactly which fact families still need
that check before a caller should treat their column semantics as
independently confirmed rather than merely upstream-documented.

## What to read next

The function reference (`?collect_point`, `?geo_point_request`,
`?collect_points`) documents every argument in full, including ones this
vignette does not exercise, such as passing an explicit `retrieved_at` for
a reproducible live run. `terroir_external_facts()` and
`terroir_fact_status()` document exactly which external-authority facts
this package asserts and which of them have been checked against their own
catalogue, family by family. `NEWS.md` describes the newest source,
`ocular`, and the cloud-masking behaviour this vignette's offline fixtures
do not exercise, in full.

## Reproduce

This vignette draws no random numbers: every value comes from the shipped
offline fixtures or from the package's own deterministic code.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
